analysis.one_liner: Opens the Arctic refuge coastal plain to oil and gas drilling, sending half the revenue to Alaska.
analysis.headline: The bill never came to a vote: introduced in May 2014, it sat in the Senate Energy Committee with no hearing, no committee vote, and no floor action until the Congress ended in January 2015.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have repealed the federal law that bans oil and gas drilling in the coastal plain of the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge and ordered the Interior Department to run competitive lease sales there, starting with at least 200,000 acres within 18 months. Half of the bonus, rental, and royalty money would have gone monthly to the state of Alaska. The bill included environmental conditions — a 2,000-acre cap on development's surface footprint, reclamation liability for drillers, and required project labor agreements — but it also directed the Interior Department not to study a no-drilling alternative in its environmental review of the first lease sale. It was referred to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee and never advanced.
analysis.who_benefits: Oil and gas companies would have gained a new drilling frontier in the Arctic refuge through mandatory lease sales. Alaska would have received 50 percent of all bonus, rental, and royalty revenues, paid monthly. Alaska Native corporations would have received conveyances of land and hiring and contracting preferences, and construction workers would have gained from required project labor agreements.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the statutory prohibition on producing oil and gas from the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge and directs the Interior Secretary to establish a competitive leasing program for the coastal plain, with a first lease sale of at least 200,000 acres within 18 months of enactment and a second sale within a year after that.
Sends 50 percent of bonus, rental, and royalty revenues from the leasing program to the state of Alaska, paid monthly, with the remainder deposited in the federal Treasury.

Attaches conditions to leases: a royalty of at least 12.5 percent, lessee liability for land reclamation, use of the best commercially available technology, a 2,000-acre cap on the surface footprint of production and support facilities, and a 'no significant adverse effect' standard for fish, wildlife, subsistence resources, and the environment.

Requires lessees and their contractors to negotiate project labor agreements and to make their best efforts to provide a fair share of employment and contracting for Alaska Natives and Alaska Native corporations.
Conveys the surface estate of certain land to the Kaktovik Inupiat Corporation and remaining subsurface estate to the Arctic Slope Regional Corporation, clearing title under earlier agreements.

analysis.who_pays: The public would have borne the environmental risk of industrial development in a protected wildlife refuge. The bill would have narrowed the environmental review by ordering the Interior Secretary not to identify or analyze a no-leasing alternative, and by declaring drilling automatically compatible with the refuge's purposes without further findings. The federal Treasury would have kept only half the revenue.
analysis.who_pays_short: The public and the Arctic refuge

drawbacks.text: The bill orders the Interior Secretary, in preparing the environmental impact statement for the first lease sale, to neither identify nor analyze nonleasing alternatives — removing the option of studying whether not to drill at all.

It declares the oil and gas leasing program and drilling activities compatible with the purposes for which the Arctic refuge was established, with no further findings or decisions required, overriding the normal refuge compatibility process.

It repeals the statutory ban on refuge drilling and forbids the Interior Secretary from closing any coastal plain land to leasing or development except under the act's own terms — a permanent change to a conservation area for a resource program whose revenues split 50/50 between Alaska and the Treasury.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is not a giveaway without strings: it includes a real royalty, a 2,000-acre surface footprint cap, reclamation liability, project labor agreements, and Alaska Native hiring preferences. But its central purpose is opening a protected wildlife refuge to drilling while limiting the environmental analysis to a single leasing alternative. The costs fall on a nationally significant conservation area and its wildlife and subsistence users, while the direct financial gains flow to whichever companies win the leases, with half the revenue to Alaska.

outcome.mechanism: Murkowski introduced the bill and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee, which took no further action before the Congress ended in January 2015, so it never got a vote in committee or on the floor.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced in the Senate on May 22, 2014, read twice, and referred to the Committee on Energy and Natural Resources.
The action history shows no further action — no hearing, no committee markup, no floor vote — through the end of the 113th Congress in January 2015.

The bill would have repealed the prohibition in the Alaska National Interest Lands Conservation Act against producing oil and gas from the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge, the change at the center of the proposal.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died without a vote, the Arctic refuge's coastal plain stayed closed to oil and gas leasing, and the oil industry did not gain access; the statutory drilling ban and existing refuge protections remained in place.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The refuge stayed closed to drilling

for.name: Sen. Lisa Murkowski
for.role: U.S. Senator from Alaska; bill sponsor

against.name: Sen. Ron Wyden
against.role: Chair, Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for committee action; it sat in committee until the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: A Republican introduced the bill with a single Democratic cosponsor, and no roll-call votes were ever taken, so the partisan shape of any real fight was never recorded.

industries.note: The bill would have opened the Arctic refuge's coastal plain to competitive lease sales, starting with at least 200,000 acres — a new drilling frontier for the companies that won the leases. The public would have gained revenue (half to Alaska) but borne the environmental risk, with the bill restricting the government's ability to even study a no-drilling option.

industries.industry: Alaska Native regional corporations (Arctic Slope Regional Corporation, Kaktovik Inupiat Corporation)
industries.note: The bill directs land conveyances to these corporations and requires lessees to give their best efforts toward a fair share of employment and contracting for Alaska Natives. Their interests in the bill ran alongside local residents' continued access to traditional-use lands, which the bill also protects.
Leases would have required project labor agreements for production, maintenance, and construction work, guaranteeing a role for organized construction labor on any development.
